fig12_1: Two side-by-side scatter plots of grid points on the unit disk, each with twenty-five radial and twenty angular points. The left panel, the naive grid, shows points densely clustered in a tight knot around the centre, with a dashed circle marking where half the points lie yet enclosing only a quarter of the disk area. The right panel, the doubled grid, spreads points far more evenly across the disk with no point at the origin, illustrating that the doubling trick distributes resolution efficiently.
fig12_2: Two panels comparing the naive and doubled radial grids. The left panel plots annulus area against radial position, showing the naive grid wastes area on extremely thin annuli near the centre while the doubled grid keeps areas balanced. The right panel is a log-log plot of maximum stable time step versus radial point count, where blue circles for the naive grid fall along a steep slope of minus four and red squares for the doubled grid follow a gentler slope of minus two, demonstrating a far less restrictive time-step constraint.
fig12_3: A grid of six color-mapped eigenmode patterns of the Laplacian on the unit disk, computed with twenty-five radial and twenty angular points. The fundamental mode is a single smooth dome of one sign, while the remaining modes show increasingly intricate Bessel-type patterns of alternating positive and negative regions separated by nodal diameters (straight node lines through the centre) and concentric nodal circles, matching classical drumhead vibration shapes.
fig12_4: Two panels validating the disk eigenvalues. The left panel plots the first twenty-five eigenvalues by index, with computed circles landing exactly on the exact squared Bessel zeros marked as crosses, and degenerate pairs for angular number at least one appearing as coincident markers. The right panel is a semilog plot of the error in the fundamental eigenvalue against radial point count, showing a straight downward line that signals exponential, spectral convergence to near machine precision.
fig12_5: A sequence of disk plots showing the single nodal diameter of the first degenerate eigenspace at eigenvalue approximately fourteen point sixty-eight. As the mixing angle phi increases, the straight node line rotates smoothly to successive orientations across the disk, over faint red and blue background shading marking positive and negative regions of the mode. The continuous rotation illustrates that any orientation is an equally valid eigenmode, reflecting the rotational symmetry of the circle.
fig12_6: A three-dimensional surface plot of the Poisson solution, the deflection of a clamped circular membrane under an off-centre Gaussian load. The surface rises to a single rounded peak located over the load position at x equals zero point four, y equals zero point two, then falls away smoothly in all directions to zero at the circular clamped rim, showing the asymmetric response to the off-centre forcing.
fig12_7: A filled contour plot of the Poisson solution over the unit disk, with color indicating deflection magnitude. A red star marks the centre of the Gaussian load, and the level curves form roughly concentric loops crowded and shifted toward the load location rather than centred on the origin, visibly distorted away from circular symmetry by the off-centre source.
fig12_8: Two panels of radial profiles of the solution at eight equally spaced angles, plotted from the clamped boundary at radius one on the left to the origin on the right, all vanishing at the boundary. In the left panel, for a centred source, the eight curves collapse exactly onto one monotone curve peaking at the origin, confirming no artificial anisotropy. In the right panel, for the off-centre source at zero point four, zero point two, the curves fan apart; the profile nearest the source direction peaks near radius zero point four-five at the source distance, while profiles pointing away stay much lower, and all return to zero at the boundary.
fig12_9: Six color-mapped snapshots of the temperature field on a circular wafer at increasing times from a cold start at time zero to steady state at time twenty. A localised hot spot forms near the laser source at x equals zero point three on the horizontal axis and grows and spreads outward through diffusion, with temperature held at zero on the circular boundary that caps the spreading, until the distribution stabilises.
fig12_10: Two panels for the heat problem. The left panel plots maximum wafer temperature against time, rising quickly then leveling off as the solution approaches steady state. The right panel overlays the radial temperature profile at angle zero from the Crank-Nicolson steady state, drawn solid, against the direct steady Poisson solve, drawn dashed; the two curves coincide, confirming the time-marched solution reaches the correct equilibrium.
